title: Looking Ahead: Con Miras A and Con Vistas A

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *para* + infinitive (A2 Unit 30), *para que* (B1 Unit 4) and *con el fin de* + infinitive (B1 Unit 32). This lesson adds two phrases for a purpose that looks ahead, often a plan or a project: *con miras a* and *con vistas a*, "with a view to". They mean the same, and both take an infinitive or a noun: *con miras a ampliar la oficina*, *con vistas a las vacaciones*. With a noun, remember that *a* + *el* becomes *al*: *con miras al verano*. *Con el fin de* also means "in order to" and normally takes an infinitive. One more pattern gives a purpose with two different subjects: *de modo que* + subjunctive, like *para que*: *Hablé despacio de modo que todos entendieran*.

sections.title: Purpose that looks ahead
rows: con miras a + infinitive or noun
con vistas a + infinitive or noun

items.spanish: Ahorramos dinero con miras a comprar una casa.
items.english: We save money with a view to buying a house.

items.spanish: El club reservó el hotel con vistas a las vacaciones de julio.
items.english: The club booked the hotel with the July holidays in mind.

items.spanish: Abrieron una oficina nueva con miras al mercado regional.
items.english: They opened a new office with the regional market in mind.

items.spanish: Cambiamos el horario de modo que todos pudieran venir.
items.english: We changed the schedule so that everyone could come.

sections.content: Use an infinitive after *con miras a* or *con vistas a* when you name what you plan to do, and a noun when you name the event: *con miras a comprar*, *con miras al viaje*. Do not change the preposition: it is always *a*, never *en* or *para*. These phrases sound planned and a little formal, so for a simple everyday purpose *para* is still the natural word. After *de modo que*, a purpose uses the subjunctive: *de modo que todos entiendan*, with the imperfect after a past verb.
